title: Impact of local shielding on microstructural defects and fatigue behaviour in L-DED repaired Ti–6Al–4V
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the influence of deposition direction and shielding environment on the fatigue performance of laser-directed energy deposition (L-DED) repair of Ti–6Al–4V. Fatigue tests and microstructural analysis show insignificant differences due to deposition direction or environment. However, locally shielded repairs exhibited fatigue initiation from oxygen-rich defects, which were absent in coupons repaired under an inert gas environment. These defects were undetectable by bulk compositional analysis or X-ray micro computed tomography and were only identified through fractography. Microscopy revealed that the defects formed during solidification, with an equiaxed microstructure and enriched in oxygen and nitrogen. They were also significantly harder and stiffer than the surrounding matrix, promoting crack initiation. These features resemble low-density inclusions or hard alpha defects known from cast Ti–6Al–4V, and this study is the first to report such defects in laser additive manufacturing. Spatter analysis and infrared imaging suggest that high-temperature particles escaped local shielding and reacted with the interstitials available in the atmosphere. Subsequent deposition resulted in incomplete melting and limited diffusion, resulting in chemically distinct inclusions. These finding highlight the critical role of environment in L-DED of Ti–6Al–4V, particularly for repair applications with limited deposition height.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the value proposition of utilizing AM to repair or refurbish aerospace components has become attractive [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ]. Out of the many AM technologies, laser directed energy deposition (L-DED) has been most prominent in the application of repair [ 8 ]. This technology has already been implemented for turbine blades and blisks [ 9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 ,  15 ,  16 – 17 ], as well as marine components [ 18 ,  19 – 20 ]. However, the application of AM repair on fatigue-critical aerospace components requires adequate structural integrity and capability for the intended usage following repair [ 21 ], and research is still ongoing to fully characterise mechanical performance after AM repair [ 22 ,  23 ,  24 ,  25 – 26 ].

Ti–6Al–4V is widely used in critical aerospace components due to its desirable properties such as high strength to weight ratio, high strength at elevated temperatures and high corrosion resistance [ 27 ]. For additively manufactured Ti–6Al–4V, it has been reported that void defects such as keyhole, gas porosity and lack-of-fusion (LOF) are the main driving factors in fatigue performance [ 28 ,  29 ,  30 ,  31 ,  32 ,  33 ,  34 ,  35 – 36 ]. However, Choi et al. show that in the absence of large LOF or surface-breaking pores, oxygen-rich defects might dominate fatigue initiation [ 37 ]. Titanium is well known for its high affinity for interstitial elements prevalent in air such as oxygen and nitrogen [ 27 ], and hence AM of titanium requires an inert gas environment [ 38 ]. When applying L-DED to repair large aerospace components, the use of an inert gas chamber can become uneconomical. Therefore, local shielding has been utilised and many studies have shown through adequate shielding nozzle design and flow rate, the effect of oxygen or nitrogen can be reduced or eliminated [ 39 ,  40 ,  41 ,  42 – 43 ]. It has been shown using a tent shielding with controlled oxygen ppm that even at 2000 ppm the mechanical properties of additively manufactured Ti–6Al–4V can be maintained at an acceptable level of hardness and elongation [ 44 ]. Despite the large number of publications in AM Ti–6Al–4V, there has been no other reports of oxygen rich defects that were observed in Choi et al. [ 37 ].

Some studies have shown crystallographic facets initiating fatigue cracks. For Ti–6Al–4V, these facets are classified as α-phase and may look like a single facet or clusters of facets [ 45 ] .  There is no compositional analysis reported for such facets but rather concluded they are similar to conventionally processed Ti–6Al–4V, where such facets are attributed to the crystallographic orientation and slip planes [ 46 ]. Higher magnification of the initiation site reveals striations and lath features without a clear distinction to the surrounding matrix and the size of the facets were closer to the size of the α grains. These features are clearly different to that observed in Choi et al. [ 37 ] or presented further in this paper. In nickel-based superalloys, the composition of such facets shows similar composition to the base material, suggesting the facets stem from the microstructure and grain orientation rather than inclusions [ 47 ,  48 ].

Oxide particles due to oxidation have been identified as a fatigue initiating defect for certain alloys such as AlSi10Mg due to vaporized metal [ 49 ]. However, to the best of the author’s knowledge, there is no reported study of oxide particles forming internally during additive manufacturing of Ti–6Al–4V. Even in a controlled build environment oxidation study by Dietrich et al. [ 50 ], fatigue initiation occurs due to porosity in both low and high oxygen concentration in the build chamber. The closest resemblance of oxygen rich defects were shown in the fractographic analysis by Akerfeldt, Pederson and Antti [ 51 ], where a LOF defect with sharp crystal like features was attributed to a thin oxide layer. However, this defect was very large (> 100 μm) and had a rough morphology resembling other LOF defects.

To make repair of Ti–6Al–4V components using L-DED a solution for future aerospace components, the effect of oxygen rich defects on fatigue properties as well as the formation mechanism of such defects must be identified and analysed. This study aims to analyse the effect on fatigue properties for such defects and provide an in-depth understanding of the defects and their formation during the L-DED repair process. This will be achieved by comparing Ti–6Al–4V coupons repaired in atmosphere with local shielding with those that are repaired in an inert gas environment. The fatigue properties and microstructure of the coupons are compared to determine whether defect formation is related to the deposition environment. Furthermore, process monitoring and spatter particle analysis results are analysed to understand the formation mechanism of such defects.

sections.heading: Material
paragraphs: The Ti–6Al–4V mill-annealed (MA) (as per AMS 4911) substrates were machined into flat plates (200 mm × 100 mm × 6.5 mm) with the composition as shown in Table  1  (chemical composition provided by the supplier). Due to the shortage of supply of substrate material, two different batches of substrates were used. From the initial investigation of microhardness and microstructure and subsequent fatigue testing of baseline material showed no significant difference between substrates. Hence all coupons were manufactured with both Ti–6Al–4V substrates. The powder used for the deposition was Ti–6Al–4V Grade 5 extra-low interstitial (ELI) 1  (composition shown in Table  1 ) supplied by TLS Technik in the form of spherical gas atomized particles in the size range of 45–90 μm. The powder was dried in an oven over 24 h prior to deposition at 100 °C. sections.heading: Laser directed energy deposition (L-DED) repair
paragraphs: L-DED repair of a single layer deposition was performed using the Trumpf TruLaser Cell 7020, with a fibre delivered 3 kW disk laser and a lens focussing system with a focal length of 250 mm. A commercial coaxial deposition nozzle was used for the deposition with an 8 mm powder focal distance. Local shielding through the coaxial deposition nozzle was utilized with no external shielding. To reflect the worst-case scenario in potential real-life application of the L-DED repair, no local pre-heating or stress relieving procedures were included in the deposition process. To determine the effect of deposition direction with respect to grind-out boundary on the formation of oxygen rich defects and subsequent fatigue properties, two different deposition directions were investigated as shown in Fig.  1 . The L-DED parameter is outlined in Table  2 . Fig. 1 Schematic of two different deposition pattern  a  Longitudinal (R1) and  b  transverse (R2) Table 2 Laser-directed energy deposition parameter Parameter Value Power 700 W Traverse speed 600 mm/min Spot size 1.5 mm Track overlap 0.75 mm Powder flow rate 2.34 g/min Carrier gas (Helium) 10 L/min Shielding gas (Argon) 16 L/min

In order to investigate the formation of defects, a two-colour pyrometer and infra-red (IR) camera was used during laser metal deposition as shown in Fig.  2 . The two colour pyrometer was installed to measure the temperature of the melt pool coaxial to the laser and the Optris PI 1 M (wavelength 0.85–1.1 μm, temperature range 500–1800 °C) was mounted on the deposition head angled at 30°. The pyrometer data was used to calibrate the emissivity of the IR camera measurements. Fig. 2 Melt pool temperature monitoring setup:  a  2 colour pyrometer data acquisition system (DAQ),  b  Optris PI 1M IR Camera,  c  instrumentation setup on L-DED deposition head

sections.heading: Inert gas chamber apparatus
paragraphs: A portable inert gas chamber was designed to provide a shielding environment for an existing system, as shown in Fig.  3 . Utilizing a portable inert gas chamber allowed for direct comparison of deposition quality and fatigue properties for locally shielded L-DED repair of Ti–6Al–4V to L-DED repair in an inert gas chamber. The chamber is manufactured with a steel base, acrylic walls and polyethylene sheets to create an inexpensive, sealed environment [ 52 ]. Oxygen level was measured using a Novatech controls 1730 series transmitter and Novatech 1231 oxygen probe. The chamber was purged with argon gas until the desired oxygen level of < 0.1 ppm was reached. Once the desired oxygen level was reached, the argon gas was continuously flown at approximately 5 L/min to ensure the oxygen level did not increase during deposition. Due to the limitation of the L-DED apparatus, both carrier gas and shielding gas were kept on during deposition inside the inert gas chamber. Fig. 3 Inert gas chamber setup for TRUMPF 7200 Trulaser system: (left) acrylic chamber with oxygen probe. Inert gas is supplied externally through dispersing mechanism (white plastic at the bottom of chamber), (right) Novatech 1730 series transmitter

In addition, to understand the formation mechanism of defects, the effect of environment on the processed powder was analysed. The deposition head was raised 450 mm such that the laser was not focused on a substrate and the deposition process was run in the different environments as shown through the diagram in Fig.  4 . This allowed collection of powder particles that had passed through the laser in the different environments to see the adequacy of local shielding of the coaxial nozzle on the powder flow. Powder was not recycled in any experiments during this study. The different types of powders analysed are outlined in Table  3 . Fig. 4 Apparatus setup diagram for powder catchment  a  in inert gas chamber and  b  in air Table 3 Name and processing type for different powders analysed Name Processing type VP Virgin powder L-air Powder passed through laser in air L-IG Powder passed through laser in inert gas environment

sections.heading: Coupon manufacture
paragraphs: A grind-out was machined to represent damage removal prior to repair as per airworthiness requirements [ 53 ] as shown in Fig.  5 a. To represent L-DED repair, a 0.8 mm grind-out was machined on a flat Ti–6Al–4V substrate of 100 mm × 200 mm plate, which was subsequently deposited with Ti–6Al–4V powder to fill over the grind-out. Three deposits of 20 mm × 21 mm were manufactured on each plate, ensuring the substrate had cooled to room temperature prior to each deposition. Once deposition was complete, the top surface of the substrate (including the laser deposit layer) was machined by 0.2 mm to result in a 0.6 mm final grind-out depth, representing a 10% grind-out without any geometric stress concentrations as shown in Fig.  5 b. After the machining process was complete, the plate was wire-cut into three sections and then machined to the final coupon dimension as shown in Fig.  6 . All coupons were machined to an N6 surface finish. Fig. 5 Schematic of substrate and coupons with  a  grind-out and  b  deposit and coupon inlayed with final surface milling Fig. 6 Dimensions of fatigue dog-bone coupon, adapted as per ASTM E466M [ 54 ]

sections.heading: Fatigue testing
paragraphs: Two different deposition direction as outlined in Fig.  1  and two different building environments (air and inert gas) were used to build test coupons. A list of all variations of test coupons are outlined in Table  4 . Table 4 Outline of specimen variations Variable No Description 1 Substrate 2 Substrate with a 0.6 mm grind-out depth R1 air As repaired (longitudinal raster pattern) in air with local shielding R2 air As repaired (transverse raster pattern) in air with local shielding R1 IG As repaired (longitudinal raster pattern) in inert gas R2 IG As repaired (transverse raster pattern) in inert gas

Coupon loads were applied cyclically using a 100 kN servo-hydraulic mechanical testing machine in a National Association of Testing Authorities (NATA) certified laboratory. The surfaces and edges of all samples were polished to 1000 grit prior to testing, and the details of the test specimens are outlined in Figs.  1  and  6  and Table  4 . Axial constant amplitude fatigue testing was performed using an R ratio of 0.1 and test frequency of 10 Hz, in accordance with ASTM standard E466 [ 54 ]. Peak stress of 500 MPa, 600 MPa and 700 MPa were tested, and net section stress was used to calculate the applied force for each coupon with the exception of the grind-out coupons, which were measured from the simulated cross sectional area if grind-out was not present. This was to represent a comparison with a repair scenario where the unexpected damage would be machined out and put back into service without any further fill-in treatment. All testing was completed at room temperature.

sections.heading: Material characterisation
paragraphs: Composition of both the powder samples outlined in Table  3  and the deposited material outlined in Table  4  were analysed using Inductively Coupled Plasma Atomic Emission Spectrometer (ICP-AES) and an elemental analyser. The deposited material was machined from coupons post-testing using a Struers Accutom-50. Due to the mass required for analysis, multiple samples of the same deposition variable were analysed for the deposited material.

Microhardness measurements were performed using a Struers Duramin-40 microhardness tester. On a polished surface, an applied load of 300 gf was held for 11s, in accordance with standard ASTM procedure E384 [ 55 ]. The hardness across the deposited layer, Heat-Affected Zone (HAZ), and substrate were taken at each 1 mm interval across the polished surface, at 0.2 mm depth interval from the machined surface up to a depth of 2.6 mm.

sections.heading: Porosity characterisation
paragraphs: X-ray micro-computed tomography (µCT) can detect a density change in material and hence is an excellent non-destructive technique to measure void defects within the sample. The adoption of µCT to detect defects in AM has shown the possibility of better understanding the defect size, location, and distribution within a sample non-destructively [ 56 ,  57 ,  58 ,  59 – 60 ]. X-Ray µCT scan of the gauge volume of the fatigue coupons was performed using a Xylon Precision µCT system equipped with a cone beam 225 kV microfocus X-ray source. The sample, particularly the deposit region, was positioned off-centre and away to avoid centreline artefacts forming in the deposit region. The µCT scan parameters were set as follows: 145 kV voltage, 110 µA current, 1000 ms integration time, 3060 total projections, 0.5 mm Copper filter, and 2.00pF panel sensitivity. The tomographic volumes were reconstructed using VGSTUDIO MAX v3.3 software, with a resulting image pixel dimension of 2480 × 2480 and a cubic voxel size of 17.77 µm. A medium projection smoothing filtration was used to reduce the noise level of the reconstructed volume. Void defect characterisation was performed using the in-built EzyPore porosity analysis package in VGSTUDIO MAX v3.3 software. Void defects that contained a total of 8 voxels or less were removed from the analysis.

In order to determine which defects initiated fatigue, µCT was also conducted on a fractured surface after fatigue failure, and geometrically registered to the original µCT measurement using the manual registration module in VGSTUDIO MAX 3.3 software.

sections.heading: Fracture surface analysis
paragraphs: Fracture surfaces were analysed using the Keyence VHX500 3D optical microscope and ThermoFisher Scientific APREO Field Emission SEM (FESEM). The composition of the fatigue initiating defects were measured using an Oxford X-Max20 Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) detector. EDS measurements were obtained at 15 kV accelerating voltage with carbon deconvolution applied. In addition, a Zeiss Merlin FESEM equipped with an Oxford X-Max Extreme 100 mm 2  windowless Silicon Drift Detector (SDD) was used to confirm the light element presence of some fracture surface samples. This detector offers the most sensitive light element detection at very low accelerating voltages. An accelerating voltage of 7 kV was used for EDS analysis.

The oxygen rich defects were not detectable using non-destructive methods such as μCT and only visible upon microscopic observation of a fracture surface [ 37 ]. These oxygen rich defects were difficult to find on a polished surface of the deposit due to occurrence of these defects being low and size of defects being small compared to the L-DED deposit volume. Therefore, all samples analysed were from a fractured surface where half of the oxygen rich defect can be observed.

sections.heading: Defect cross section preparation
paragraphs: To obtain accurate analysis of the defects, fracture surfaces were cross-sectioned with the Struers Accutom-10 as close as possible to the defect. Then the specimen was mounted in Struers Epofix resin and polished to a 0.25 μm finish to the defect location. A final polishing step of (colloidal silica) OP-S solution was used to reveal the microstructure and to prepare the sample for Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD). Once specimens were polished, they were broken out of the mounting resin and cleaned with acetone and then ethanol for analysis. An example fracture surface and schematic of sectioned surface extraction is given in Fig.  7 . Fig. 7 a  Overview of a fracture surface showing a crack initiating defect,  b  schematic of the fracture sample extraction for microstructural analysis,  c  schematic of the microstructural analysis of sectioned surface and analysis area around crack initiating defect

Additionally, a blind hole with a depth of 2 mm was drilled into a Struers PolyFast blank mount in order to analyse the microstructure of the processed powders listed in Table  3 . The blind hole was filled with powder mixed with the Struers Epofix resin for the different powders. Once the Epofix and powder mixture was set, the mounts were polished with 320 grit grinding paper, 9 µm diamond paste and a final polishing step with OPS to reveal the microstructure. To reduce the charging the polished powder samples were coated with 10 nm of carbon with a Leica EM ACE600 sputter coater.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterisation
paragraphs: Samples were cross-sectioned, mounted, and polished to a 0.25 μm finish. A final polishing step of OP-S (colloidal silica) solution was used to reveal the microstructure. To reveal the macrostructure, the polished surface was subsequently etched using Kroll’s solution (92% distilled water, 6% Nitric Acid, 2% Hydrofluoric acid). The macrostructure was analysed using an Olympus GX53 inverted optical microscope.

The microstructure and composition of polished samples of the deposit, powders and the defects were analysed using a JEOL JSM-7200F FESEM equipped with a solid-state backscatter electron (BSE) detector, an Oxford X-Max20 EDS Detector and an Oxford Symmetry EBSD Detector. EBSD orientation maps were obtained at a 20 kV accelerating voltage, a current of ~ 20nA and a step size of 0.06 ~ 0.25 µm. The binning was varied depending on the polished surface quality and required final map area.

On the polished defect, the FEI Scios Dualbeam Focused Ion Beam SEM (FIBSEM) was used to extract Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) samples of the defect. The JEOL JEM-2100 FEGTEM equipped with Tridium Gatan Imaging Filter was used to collect electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) spectrum.

In addition, nano indentation measurements were performed using the Hysitron TI-950 with a Berkovich indentation probe. An applied load of 7 mN was loaded in a trapezoidal loading and unloading pattern over 60 s to obtain the elastic modulus and hardness of each indent.

sections.heading: Spatter particle analysis procedure
paragraphs: To understand whether spatter affects the oxygen rich defect formation, L-DED deposit and the surrounding surfaces were analysed in an FEI Scios Dualbeam FIBSEM equipped with an Oxford X-MAX80 EDS detector. The FIBSEM was used to obtain cross-sectional view of the spatter particles.

sections.heading: Composition
paragraphs: The measured composition of the powders show a slight increase in oxygen when the powder is passed through the laser, whether it is in air or in an inert gas chamber. However, the level of oxygen pickup between the inert gas chamber and in air with local shielding is within the allowed limits of AMS4911 compositional requirement of Ti–6Al–4V (Table  5 ). The measured composition of the deposited Ti–6Al–4V material shows a slight increase in oxygen concentration in R1 Air and R2 IG that is noncompliant to AMS4911 compositional requirement of Ti–6Al–4V (Table  5 ). However, considering the inert gas environment of R2 IG would have minimal oxygen interaction, this is potentially an effect of the sample preparation process due to the limited number of samples for R1 IG and R2 IG. For these samples, the deposited material of 0.5 mm thickness had to be precisely machined off a fatigue test coupon post-fracture and hence could have introduced additional oxygen through surface oxide levels. Overall, the difference between Air and IG in both powder and deposit is minimal, indicating local shielding is sufficient in protecting the deposited material during L-DED repair of Ti–6Al–4V. sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: A good metallurgical bond is observed for all L-DED repair samples with a smooth transition between the deposit repair, HAZ and substrate. No micro-cracking is observed for any samples, as shown in Fig.  8 . The microstructure of the deposited layer shows columnar grains directed outward from the substrate, similar to published literature [ 62 ,  63 – 64 ], which indicates a cooling direction. There are slightly dark coloured bands that formed at the interface of each track (Fig.  8 a and c). However, the dilution was sufficient for the given process parameters that there are no distinct track lines obvious within the HAZ region. These track lines are not visible in the microstructure of R2, as shown in Fig.  8 b and d since the track direction is parallel to the cross-sectional view in this case. The deposit and HAZ depth are similar for all R1 and R2 microstructures for the air and inert gas coupons, which indicates the input energy was similar regardless of deposition direction or environment. The microstructure observed in the SEM also shows all R1 Air, R2 Air R1 IG and R2 IG have a lamellar (α + β) microstructure, as shown in Fig.  9  with alpha lath widths ranging from 0.1 to 1 μm similar to that reported in [ 37 ]. Fig. 8 Etched microstructure of cross-sectional view for  a  R1 Air  b  R2 Air  c  R1 IG and  d  R2 IG Fig. 9 Microstructure observed in SEM of both R1 and R2 for L-DED repair deposit in air and inert gas chamber

sections.heading: Microhardness
paragraphs: The average microhardness through depth for all R1 Air, R2 Air, R1 IG and R2 IG are shown in Fig.  10 . Minor variation in average hardness was observed in the deposited layer between 370 and 390 HV, which gradually reduced to 330–350 HV through the HAZ to the substrate. The difference in microhardness between deposition with local shielding and deposition in inert gas environment is minimal. All samples show a higher microhardness in the deposited layer and HAZ when compared to the substrate. The results support the similarities observed in microstructure between all deposits as shown in Figs.  8  and  9 . The microhardness of substrates are comparable to nominal Ti–6Al–4V (340 HV) [ 27 ]. The microhardness of the deposited layer is higher than the mill annealed substrate due to the high cooling rates in AM developing finer microstructures. The results here are comparable to that reported in the literature of L-DED Ti–6Al–4V of 360–420 HV [ 65 ,  66 ]. Fig. 10 Average microhardness measurement of deposit layer through to the substrate

To understand if different deposition direction would affect the microhardness, a map of the microhardness is shown in Fig.  11 . Despite the different deposition directions, no significant difference is observed in the peaks and troughs of the microhardness distribution across the deposit, HAZ and substrate. Fig. 11 Microhardness map of  a  R1 Air,  b  R2 Air,  c  R1 IG,  d  R2 IG

sections.heading: Powder analysis
paragraphs: Powder that passed through the laser in both air and an inert gas environment was collected, analysed and compared to virgin powder. Both the EDS compositional analysis and microstructure show a lack of difference between the powders, which indicate the local shielding from the coaxial nozzle is sufficient in protecting the powders that have been processed through the laser (Fig.  12 ). Fig. 12 Backscatter SEM images of  a ,  d  Virgin powder,  b ,  e  L-IG and  c ,  f  L-Air

sections.heading: Porosity analysis
paragraphs: To understand if the fatigue initiating defects correlated to porosity distribution of the coupons, an overlay of the defects from the µCT scan and the fracture surface is shown in Fig.  13 . The µCT scan of R1 coupons showed a higher number of defects aligned with the deposit track edges near the boundaries of the machined grind-out groove, indicating the formation of inter-track porosity at the curvature of the grind-out. In comparison, R2 showed very little inter-track porosity indicating R2 build direction was not affected by the grind-out. The deposition strategy was programmed assuming that there was no change in deposit height. Therefore, it seems likely the curvature of the grind-out and change in stand-off distance caused misalignment of the laser and powder focus forming incompatible aspect ratios of the deposited layer resulting in inter-track porosity. However, if this is the case, then we should observe similarly high inter-track porosity for R2 coupons near the grind-out edges. This was not observed in our results, as shown in Fig.  13 b and d. Another possible reason is that the shielding gas flow is not optimized to the different stand-off heights at the grind-out which causes porosity. However, a study conducted on the shielding gas of gas metal arc welding [ 67 ] concluded that the stand-off distance had minimal impact with a sufficient gas flow rate of > 9L/min. Fig. 13 µCT scan and defect data geometrically registered onto the fracture surface for  a  R1 Air  b  R2 Air  c  R1 IG and  d  R2 IG (Blue arrow is scanning direction and red circle showing grind-out curvature area)

An alternative reason could be turbulence created by the shielding gas as it approaches the grind-out boundary as illustrated in Fig.  14 . R1 constantly moves in and out of the grind-out boundary, whereas R2 deposits along the direction resulting in less interaction between the grind-out boundary and the shielding gas flow. The conical shielding gas flow becomes complex as it approaches a step height, with studies of even simplified flow models showing complexity in approaching or leaving a step height [ 68 ,  69 ]. Although there have been studies on shielding gas in LMD, these are limited to studies of gas flow rates or modifying shielding apparatus to optimize shielding for additive manufacturing on a flat substrate [ 70 ]. Fig. 14 Diagram of shielding gas flow affected by approaching grind-out edge

Figure  13  also showed that the samples deposited in the inert gas chamber have significantly greater inter-track porosity and gas porosity when compared to the samples deposited in air. Although the external gas flow is minimal during deposition (5 L/min to the whole chamber to keep O 2  level < 0.1 ppm), it is possible that the local shielding gas flow from the nozzle was disrupted by the external gas flow into the chamber. To reduce the effect of external gas flow, the chamber was designed for the external gas to be dispersed through multiple inlets throughout the chamber. However, due to the limitation of chamber size, the inlet flow could still interact with the shielding gas flow. It has been reported in the presence of cross-flow the shielding gas flow will have a different flow characteristic [ 71 ]. Modification of carrier and shielding gas is limited due to the in-built control system of the deposition apparatus, hence turning the gas off was not possible. In addition to the complex shielding gas flow approaching a step height, the effect of cross-flow could explain the increased porosity in coupons deposited in the inert gas chamber.

sections.heading: Fatigue test results and analysis
paragraphs: The fatigue testing results are presented in Fig.  15 . The coupon testing results from this study are compared with mill annealed Ti–6Al–4V casting from the metallic materials properties development (MMPDS) [ 72 ]. The results of the baseline testing are comparable despite the thickness and microstructural difference. The fatigue testing results show all laser repaired coupons have much shorter fatigue lives compared to the baseline results. However, both R1 Air and R2 Air coupons have consistently longer lives than the standard grind-out coupons for higher peak stress levels of 700 MPa. At the lower peak stress levels of 500 MPa and 600 MPa, the fatigue lives of the AM repaired Ti–6Al–4V coupons were within the scatter range as the ground-out repair results. The fatigue results of R1 and R2 repaired Ti–6Al–4V coupons do not show a distinct difference, indicating the direction of deposition to the loading direction or grind-out profile has an insignificant effect on the fatigue performance. R1 IG and R2 IG were only tested at peak stress of 600 MPa due to resource limitations. Fig. 15 Fatigue life of R1 Air, R2 Air, R1 IG and R2 IG L-DED repair coupons overlaid with MMPDS [ 72 ]

sections.heading: Fracture surface analysis
paragraphs: Fractography of the fracture surface indicated a few different types of fatigue initiating features: oxygen rich defects, lack-of-fusion (LOF), gas porosity, and microstructural defects as shown in Fig.  16 . Nomenclature of the flat cleavage-looking defects similar to Fig.  16 a as an oxygen rich defect taken from Choi et al. [ 37 ]. Some of the defects could be surface breaking, as shown in Fig.  16 e. Fig. 16 Fractography images of the different types of fatigue initiating features:  a  Oxygen rich defect,  b  spherical porosity,  c  microstructural defect,  d  lack-of-fusion,  e  surface breaking oxygen rich defect,  f  surface breaking lack-of-fusion and  g  microstructural defect on edge

The results from the Oxford X-Max20 and X-Max Extreme 100 mm 2  windowless SDD on the fracture surface for an oxygen rich defect are shown in Fig.  17 . The limited energy range in the SEM equipped with the X-Max Extreme EDS resulted in lower-than-expected composition for aluminium and vanadium. Although traditional EDS methods are known to have limitations in detecting light elements such as O and N [ 73 ,  74 ], this limitation is overcome in the windowless Extreme EDS with a higher sensitivity at lower keV resulting in better detection of light elements [ 75 ]. This is confirmed from the higher counts in the lower energy region of the spectrum. However, this results in a comparatively lower detection of heavier elements due to the lower energy level used. Despite this, both detectors confirm a significant difference in composition between the defect region and the surrounding matrix, with the defect region having higher O and N contents, confirming these are the same type of defects observed in Choi et al. [ 37 ]. Fig. 17 EDS spectra results from defect and surrounding region for both EDS X-Max20 and EDS X-Max Extreme showing elevated N and O concentration in Defect region

For the coupons deposited in air, majority failed from oxygen rich defects (Fig.  18 ). With the use of an inert gas chamber, the oxygen rich defects are eliminated. It is difficult to ascertain whether oxygen rich defects influence fatigue life or not due to the increased porosity of inert gas chamber coupons, as shown in Fig.  13 . Regardless of the impact on fatigue life, the results show changing the environment changes the fatigue initiating defect type, as shown in Fig.  18 . Fig. 18 Histogram of type of defect initiating fatigue failure (number of coupons observed are listed on top of each bar)

The porosity and fracture surface overlay show that fatigue initiates from the defects detectable by X-ray µCT when deposited in an inert gas chamber. The detectability of the fatigue initiating defect can be seen on the fracture surface overlay image shown in Fig.  19 . The coupons deposited in the air failed from oxygen rich defects, that were undetected by X-ray µCT, whilst the coupons deposited in the inert gas chamber show fatigue initiating from pore defects measuring 40–100 µm in diameter. As there is no significant difference in composition between coupons deposited in air and coupons deposited in the inert gas chamber (Table  5 ), it seems that direct detection of oxygen rich defects may not be possible with conventional quality assurance tests. Therefore, even though we cannot ascertain whether oxygen rich defects influence fatigue life or not, it is still imperative that these the formation mechanism of such defects are understood to minimize their occurrence in L-DED Ti–6Al–4V repair. Fig. 19 Fracture surface overlaid with defects measured by X-ray CT for  a  R1 Air  b  R2 Air  c  R1 IG and  d  R2 IG

A collection of fracture surface images of the oxygen rich defects are shown in Fig.  20 . The oxygen rich defects all form in the L-DED deposit area, mostly away from the machined surface. The high magnification SEM show an evident difference in fracture morphology between the defect and surrounding matrix (Fig.  20 d–f). The defect size and shape varied between oblong, circular and number eight-shaped but were generally of a smooth-edged shape. Some defects showed small spherical pores adjacent to the defect (Fig.  20 e). Higher magnification images of the defect in Fig.  21  showed brittle fracture characteristics similar to those reported for glass [ 76 ] and metallic glass [ 77 ]. Such features include but are not limited to: velocity ‘hackle’ lines that run parallel to direction of crack propagation (Fig.  21 b), micro cracking within the defect (Fig.  21 c), micro steps running parallel to the direction of crack propagation (Fig.  21 c), hackle with cross over (Fig.  21 c), wake hackle at grain boundaries (Fig.  21 d) and ‘Wallner’ lines (Fig.  21 d). Fig. 20 a – c  Overview of fracture surfaces showing clear initiation from single point with  d – f  zoom-in SEM image of initiating defect Fig. 21 High magnification images of defect showing brittle fracture characteristics.  a  overview of defect outlining location of high magnification image,  b  region showing velocity ′hackle′ lines,  c  defect fracture showing microcracking, microsteps and crossover hackle,  d  wake hackle at grain boundaries due to transgranular fracture

The fracture morphology seems similar to fish eye defects from alpha colony packets reported by Law and Blackburn [ 78 ] with some similarities also observed with initiating facets observed in lamellar Ti–6Al–4V [ 79 ]. The most similar morphology of fatigue initiating defects were from Sun et al. [ 80 ], where fatigue initiation occurred in internal defects from alpha–beta (α + β) colonies. However, the aforementioned studies do not show any evidence of compositional difference to the matrix nor a defined outlined of a defect as shown in this study.

sections.heading: Defect cross section analysis
paragraphs: The cross-section of the defect was excised, polished and analysed as per Fig.  7 . The microstructure was analysed using the backscatter SEM. There are a few features that distinguish the defect to the surrounding matrix (Fig.  22 ). Firstly, the defects show a distinctly different equiaxed microstructure compared to the lamellar and/or basketweave microstructure of the surrounding matrix (Fig.  22 a). Despite this distinct difference in microstructure, a good metallurgical bond between the defect and surrounding matrix is observed, indicating the defect formed during solidification of the molten metal. Secondly, the defects show a generally darker colour on the backscatter image, indicating the defects consists of lighter elements. This is corroborated by the EDS maps data as shown in Fig.  23 , where the defect area shows a higher concentration of oxygen and nitrogen (light elements) and lower content of aluminium. Fig. 22 Backscatter SEM image and corresponding secondary electron image of defect cross section showing distinct microstructure in defect whilst complete fusion between defect and surrounding material.  a ,  d  Defect with cracking with red rectangle marking TEM location,  b ,  e  defect with small spherical pore and  c ,  f  defect with shrinkage porosity Fig. 23 EDS compositional map of defect (Fig.  22 c) showing areas of concentration of each element

All defects analysed showed the above-mentioned features, but they also varied in size and shape in their cross-sectional view. In addition, different features from different defects are apparent, with some defects showing cracking (Fig.  22 d), some showing small amount of spherical porosity (Fig.  22 e) and some showing a cluster of shrinkage porosity (Fig.  22 f). Difference in grain size and microstructure is also apparent (Fig.  22 a–c), with some defects also showing a distinct boundary of equiaxed grains between the defect and surrounding matrix (Fig.  22 c).

EBSD shows the defect area characterised as mostly Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) titanium with small areas of retained cubic structure, as shown in Fig.  24 b. Although EBSD can only characterise the crystal structure that is pre-selected and in the database, the defect area is able to be characterized, showing it is crystalline α phase (HCP) titanium. Fig. 24 An analysed defect with  a  backscatter detector microstructure,  b  phase statistic and  c  IPF-Z

A TEM slice was taken from the middle of the defect cross-section (red rectangular box as shown in Fig.  22 a). A point EELS analysis was taken in the middle of a grain in the TEM slice as shown in Fig.  25 a. It was difficult to determine the oxygen concentration due to the overlap of vanadium and oxygen peaks. However, a small peak at the nitrogen K-edge energy level of 402 eV was detectable. This again corroborates the concentration of nitrogen in the defect area measured by Extreme EDS in Fig.  17  and the EDS Maps shown in Fig.  23 . Fig. 25 a  TEM point EELS location in the middle of grain,  b  EELS high level spectrum showing nitrogen, titanium, vanadium and oxygen peaks

A map of the hardness and elastic modulus of the defect and surrounding area show the defect is very hard and stiff compared to the surrounding matrix (Fig.  26 ). It has been reported that the average hardness of Ti–6Al–4V can range between 4.9 and 8.1 GPa, whilst oxygen enriched α case layer can range between 8.4 and 12.1 GPa [ 81 ]. Increase in nitrogen or oxygen can increase the hardness, as observed in commercially pure titanium [ 82 ] as well as α + β titanium alloys [ 83 ]. Therefore, the hardness results indicate the defect region has similar hardness of α case or nitrogen and/or oxygen enriched inclusions (Fig.  27 ). Fig. 26 a  SEM image of the region of hardness indents showing defect location at the edge of hardness indentation map;  b  Contour map of hardness map in the measured area showing peak hardness of 10–17 GPa at defect location compared to 4–7 GPa in surrounding matrix (single point with low hardness on defect due to hardness indent located on a void);  c  Contour map of elastic modulus in the measured area showing peak modulus of 190 GPa and surrounding region of 110–120 GPa, and  d  secondary electron image showing a void in defect at which low hardness and modulus is detected on the hardness map Fig. 27 Thermal monitoring data of L-DED process showing high temperature spatter particles moving outside local shielding gas area. (Each image taken at 10ms intervals)

The elastic modulus of the surrounding matrix is within the range published in the MMPDS handbook for wrought annealed Ti–6Al–4V of 107.5 ~ 128 GPa [ 72 ], whilst the defect are shows a rapid increase up to 190 GPa. This will promote crack growth due to the stress concentration induced by an elastic mismatch [ 84 ].

sections.heading: Melt pool monitoring
paragraphs: The melt pool monitoring data from the IR camera shows multiple high temperature spatter particles moving at high velocities away from the local shielding area during deposition. The temperature of the spatter particles ranges from 1000 to 1800 °C. Due to the relatively low frame rate (100 Hz) and limited spatial resolution, it was not possible to determine the speed of the high temperature spatter particles, nor the projected path. Despite these limitations, the IR camera results confirm high temperature spatter particles moving away from the shielding gas concentrated on the melt pool, potentially interacting with air, which is abundant in oxygen and nitrogen.

sections.heading: Spatter analysis
paragraphs: The melt pool monitoring data showed that multiple high temperature spatter particles were ejected from the melt pool during deposition. An EDS spot analysis also showed that some spatter particles have higher oxygen and nitrogen content whilst other spatter particles showed a lower oxygen concentration. The morphology of a Ti–6Al–4V spatter particle is like a solid spherical droplet with a smooth surface as shown in Fig.  28 b. The morphology of the spatter particles with higher oxygen and nitrogen is more porous looking with dendritic formation as shown in Fig.  28 c. The spatter particles with high oxygen and nitrogen were spontaneously distributed amongst the Ti–6Al–4V smooth spherical droplets, with more located as the spatter particles were further away from the deposit at roughly 3–10 mm. There were multiple different morphologies of the spatter particles with high oxygen and nitrogen as shown in Fig.  29 . Fig. 28 a  SEM image of the deposit and the Ti–6Al–4V spatter particles,  b  magnified view of low oxygen spatter particle and  c  magnified view of high oxygen and nitrogen spatter particle Fig. 29 SEM image of different morphologies of spatter particles  a ,  e ,  i  very fine porous microspheres (~ 1µm),  b ,  f ,  j  dendritic substructure  c ,  g ,  k  globular nodules with internal very fine porous and dendritic substructure and  d ,  h ,  l  globular dendritic platelets

Selected spatter particles were analysed by FIB milling to show the cross section of a spatter particle (Fig.  30 ). The cross sectional view of a spatter particle showed a network of internal porosity which were less than 1 μm in thickness (Fig.  30 c), and dendritic microstructure (Fig.  30 e). EDS analysis on the cross section (Fig.  30 f) detected elevated levels of nitrogen and some segregation of aluminium, similar to Fig.  23 . This indicates the high likelihood of such spatter particles partially dissolving into the deposition, but retaining the complex internal porosity and composition. Fig. 30 Cross sectional view of individual spatter particles:  a  top view of FIB location,  b ,  c  cross sectional view of spatter particle showing internal pores,  d ,  e  equivalent backscatter image of cross section showing fine dendritic microstructure,  f  EDS spectrum and composition of cross section,  g  EDS Maps showing compositional distribution

sections.heading: Defect type
paragraphs: The effect of oxygen and nitrogen during AM of titanium has been investigated but most investigate bulk property or surface layer oxidation and report no significant mechanical strength differences [ 85 ,  86 ,  87 – 88 ]. However, a previous study has shown that small localized diffusion and contamination of nitrogen and oxygen can cause detrimental effects on fatigue properties [ 37 ]. The fatigue testing results also show the occurrence fatigue initiation from such defects is very high in locally shielded L-DED Ti–6Al–4V repairs.

The microstructure and local aluminium depletion as shown in Sect.  3.8  is similar to that shown in nitrided Ti–6Al–4V, where an outer layer of TiN is formed, which progressively transitions to a nitrogen diffused α-Ti [ 89 ]. The high magnification SEM images of the defect show that there are dendritic structures within the defect (Fig.  21 ). These are similar to that reported for TiN dendrites embedded in titanium [ 90 ]. The increase in hardness (Fig.  26 ) is also evidence of nitrogen and oxygen diffusion, where the defect clearly shows an increased hardness compared to the surrounding matrix.

These defects are not new, as they appear to be similar to those defects that were extensively studied by the aerospace industry typically appearing during melting, casting and forging of titanium [ 91 ,  92 – 93 ]. They are similar in their morphology and characteristics to that classified as low-density inclusions (LDI) or hard alpha [ 27 ]. Despite the occurrence of these defects being low, these defects are critical and require to be detectable or eliminated, as shown by the advisory circular from the Federal Aviation Association [ 94 ].

sections.heading: Defect formation
paragraphs: It has been shown in Fig.  18  that coupons manufactured in an inert gas environment do not fail from the oxygen rich defects. This implies the formation of such defects is directly related to the build environment, which is not surprising due to the high affinity of titanium for oxygen and nitrogen.

The powder analysis in Sect.  3.4  shows the local shielding from the coaxial nozzle is sufficient to protect the powders heated up through the laser when the powders do not interact with the substrate. Published literature indicates the shielding gas effectiveness reduces dramatically at heights above the co-axial nozzle outlet [ 39 ,  95 ]. The observation in Fig.  27  shows that many particles are ejected above the co-axial nozzle outlet at temperatures above the β transus and sometimes above the melting temperature of Ti–6Al–4V. Zeng et al. [ 96 ] studied titanium and nitrogen interaction using in-situ X-ray diffraction tests. The results showed at an equivalent energy density of 33 J/mm 2  (the energy density calculated for the process parameters used in this study [ 37 ]), a complete TiN layer is formed within 0.6 s once temperature reaches the melting point of titanium [ 96 ]. Literature has shown even at temperatures lower than the β transus of Ti–6Al–4V, a compound layer of TiO 2 , Ti 2 N and TiN, and a diffusion zone of α titanium phase with dissolved nitrogen and oxygen is formed [ 89 ,  97 ]. In addition, the β transus temperature of Ti–6Al–4V alloys can be raised by oxygen concentration [ 98 ]. Therefore, even with the short interaction time with ambient atmosphere at high temperatures, it is likely the particles ejected above the co-axial nozzle formed compound layers of TiO 2 , Ti 2 N and TiN, which is confirmed through the EDS results in Fig.  28 . The morphology of the spatter particles observed on the substrate surface in Fig.  29  also show similarities to the dendritic morphology of the oxygen rich defects on the fracture surface (Fig.  21 ).

Spatter formation in laser welding is well known, which is the source of quality problems common to all welding. Spatter is the “ ejection from a melt pool as a result of high levels of acceleration in directions approximately perpendicular to the melt liquid surface ” [ 99 ]. As can be observed in the IR camera results in Fig.  27 , spatter also forms during laser metal deposition. More recently, the formation of spatter has been observed through in-situ high speed cameras during the L-DED process [ 100 ,  101 – 102 ]. Although these studies investigated different materials, the formation of spatter during L-DED can be observed.

Although the local shielding in L-DED of Ti–6Al–4V has been prevalent, the lack of reporting alpha case-like defects is curious. The phase diagram in Fig.  31  shows that increase in nitrogen (and/or oxygen) in Ti64 will significantly increase the liquidus temperature. During deposition, a spatter particle that has interacted with air, resulting in oxygen and nitrogen diffused titanium, may land on the substrate and interact with the laser again. On the first layer, the laser power may be insufficient to completely remelt this particle with higher oxygen or nitrogen due to the higher liquidus temperature. The laser power is sufficient to form a melt pool of Ti–6Al–4V and allow diffusion of oxygen and nitrogen from the spatter particle surface, explaining the complete metallurgical bond between the contaminated spatter particle and the surrounding matrix, as shown in Fig.  22 . However, this diffusion is limited due to the limited time at a high enough temperature. When building fatigue or tensile coupons using L-DED, subsequent layers are deposited to manufacture sufficient thickness. With subsequent deposition of layers, the contaminated spatter particles will experience multiple thermal cycles, allowing further diffusion of oxygen and/or nitrogen into the surrounding matrix. In addition, for L-DED test coupons, the deposited layers are machined away from the substrate, consequently resulting in material without the initial layer. This is likely why such oxygen and nitrogen rich defects are not reported for L-DED of Ti–6Al–4V. Fig. 31 Phase diagram of Ti–6Al–4V with increasing N (wt%) concentration showing increasing liquidus temperature with increased N concentration using PANDAT [ 103 ]

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The effect of deposition direction and environment for L-DED repaired Ti–6Al–4V have been investigated. The results show no significant differences in microstructure or fatigue performance based on deposition direction or environment. However, while fatigue life was unaffected by the deposition environment, the type of fatigue-initiating defect differed.

Fatigue initiation in locally shielded L-DED coupons predominantly originated from oxygen-rich defects, whereas no such defects were observed in coupons repaired under an inert gas environment. These oxygen-rich defects could not be detected using bulk compositional analysis or μCT, but were identified only through post-test fractography.

The defects exhibited full metallurgical bonding with the surrounding matrix, indicating formation during solidification. They displayed an equiaxed microstructure, distinct from the basketweave microstructure of the surrounding matrix. EDS revealed elevated oxygen and nitrogen concentrations and aluminium depletion, while EELS further confirmed the nitrogen enrichment. Nanohardness measurements showed the defect region were significantly harder and stiffer than the surrounding matrix, explaining their propensity to act as fatigue initiation sites. These defects resemble low-density inclusions or hard alpha defects known in cast Ti–6Al–4V. This study is the first to report such defects in laser additively manufactured Ti–6Al–4V.

A travelling IR camera recorded high-temperature spatter particles escaping the locally shielded region. Analysis of the deposit confirmed these spatter particles exhibited morphologies consistent with the solidification of metal oxides. EDS analysis showed high oxygen and nitrogen content in the particles. It is hypothesized that these spatter particles landed on the substrate and were overlaid in subsequent deposition. Due to their elevated oxygen and nitrogen content, these particles exhibited a higher melting temperature, and the laser energy was insufficient to fully melt and diffuse these particles into the deposit.

These findings demonstrate the critical importance of shielding gas integrity in L-DED of Ti–6Al–4V, particularly for repair applications with limited deposition height, where fatigue initiating hard alpha defects can form and potentially limit fatigue performance.
